Question #2
```{r}
rep(c("A","B"), each = 2)
rep(c("A","B"), times = 2)
```
each = Repeats the individual elements inside the vector,
times = Repeats the entire vector,

Question #3
```{r}
seq(1, 20, by = 2)
seq(1, 20, length.out = 5)
```
by = This controls the increment between the numbers and you can use this if you know the precise increment needed between values.

length.out = Controls all the elements and gets the exact number stated and use this to repeat values until a specific total length is reached.

Question #5
Negative indexing is best when you know the position of the element you want to remove, for example removing a certain item from your list of expenses. Logical indexing is best when you want to filter by a condition, for example keeping only the shopping items that cost 1000 pesos or less.

PART E
```{r}
inventory <- list(item = c("Notebook", "Pen", "Eraser"), price = c(25.50, 10.00, 5.00), in_stock = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE))

inventory$item[inventory$in_stock]
```
```{r}
inventory$item     <- append(inventory$item, "Ruler")
inventory$price    <- append(inventory$price, 15.00)
inventory$in_stock <- append(inventory$in_stock, TRUE)
```

Question #12
inventory$in_stock extracts the logical vector, while inventory$item extracts the character vector

Question #13
Sorting, passing data around, and adding or deleting entries can all cause mismatches when the vectors are separate. Keeping related fields together in a list prevents these errors.

CONCLUSION
A vector stores many values of the same data type, so it works well for calculations and simple filtering. A list can combine different types and structures. Use a vector when your values are all the same kind and you need to do math on them, and use a list when you want to keep different kinds of data together.
